name: 2.5 Measures of the Center of the Data
_note: Complete on disk -- 12 questions. Seven were written 2026-08-09 to finish the section. The distinctive skill here is estimating a mean from a GROUPED table using class midpoints, which nothing in the bank covered; class boundaries are constrained so no seed produces a recurring midpoint. Three slots are reused. The seven new ones cover the weighted mean, sample versus population, recovering a value from a known mean, combining two groups of different sizes (where averaging the averages is the classic error), what one extreme value does to each measure, the mode as the only center a categorical variable has, and reading all three off a drawn dot plot.

questions.title: Mean from a Grouped Frequency Table - Estimate the mean of data grouped into class intervals using class midpoints, and identify why the result is an estimate
Mean, Median and Mode from a Frequency Table - Compute the sample mean, median and mode from a frequency table, then identify which measure resists an added extreme value
Compute Mean from Fifty Values - Given 50 state-level mean commute times, compute the overall mean
Mean, Median, IQR, and Range from a Small Data Set - Compute four summary statistics from a randomized list of 9 values
Choose a Resistant Measure for a Skewed Distribution - Decide whether to report the mean+SD or median+IQR based on shape, then explain why
Mean, Median and Mode from a Dot Plot - Read the counts off a drawn dot plot, then produce all three measures of center from the same picture and say which one the tallest stack gives you
When the Mode Is the Only Center - Name the mode of a categorical variable, say why the mean and median cannot be computed for it, and identify a numeric data set that has two modes
Find a Missing Value from the Mean - Turn a known mean back into a total, subtract the values you have to recover the one that is missing, then say what happens to the mean if that value is raised
Weighted Mean of a Course Grade - Build the contribution column of a weighted mean, total it, and say why the answer differs from the plain average of the four category scores
Mean of Two Combined Groups - Recover each group's total from its mean and size, combine them to get the overall mean, and see why averaging the two means is wrong when the groups differ in size
What One Extreme Value Does to the Mean and the Median - Compute both measures of center, replace one value with a far larger one, recompute both, and see which measure moved and which did not

Sample Mean Versus Population Mean - Compute the mean of a whole group and the mean of a sample drawn from it, attach the right symbol to each, and say which one is a parameter and which is a statistic
